# Access as code

![](../images/spot-5.svg){.spot fig-alt="A gate with a yellow lintel, three pods and a sheet of paper on a mint tile. An elephant in a vest checks a clipboard."}
Pulumi checks its program against a state file, so a grant changed by hand on the server stays
invisible until a refresh, while pgsesame keeps no state and reads the catalog on every plan. The
lab wrote the same small access model with both tools to see where they differ. Either way the rules live in a file and a change is a reviewed diff,
which beats grants typed into a server once and never explained.

## One model, written twice

Both tools describe the same model:

- two group roles, `app_ro` (read) and `app_rw` (read and write), that cannot log in
- usage on the schema, and grants on its tables and sequences, for the group roles
- **default privileges**, so that tables the `app` role creates later get the same grants (the part
  hand-made setups most often forget)
- two login users, `reporter` and `ingest`, who get access only through membership in a group role

Tables, schemas and extensions stay out, because they belong to the application and its migrations.

## Pulumi keeps state and shows a diff {#pulumi-state-and-a-diff}

`pulumi/__main__.py` builds the model with `pulumi-postgresql`, a bridge to the provider that
Terraform uses, and `pulumi up` applies what `pulumi preview` shows:

```bash
pulumi preview            # what would change
pulumi up
pulumi preview --refresh  # drift check: re-read the database first
```

A plain `preview` compares the program with the state file rather than the database, which is why
hand-made changes appear only with `--refresh`. The grants also have to be chained with
`depends_on`, because the provider runs them in parallel and Postgres then fails with "tuple
concurrently updated".

## pgsesame reads the server instead {#pgsesame-one-yaml-file-no-state}

[pgsesame](https://github.com/almostly/pgsesame) declares the same model in `pgsesame/spec.yaml`, and
its `plan` reads the database catalog and prints the SQL that would make the server match the spec:

```yaml
principals:
  app_ro:
    type: role
    privileges:
      schemas: {usage: [public]}
      tables: {select: [public.*]}
  reporter:
    type: user
    password_env: SESAME_REPORTER_PASSWORD
    member_of: [app_ro]

default_privileges:
  - owner: app
    schema: public
    grantee: app_ro
    tables: [select]
```

```bash
sesame plan     # exit code 2 means there are changes
sesame apply    # one transaction: 32 statements on a fresh server
sesame plan     # empty: nothing drifted
sesame import   # write a spec from what a server grants today
```

Destructive changes (revokes, drops and changes of owner) need explicit flags, and passwords come
from environment variables, never from the file.

## Side by side

| | Pulumi | pgsesame |
|---|---|---|
| source of truth | a Python program plus a state file | one YAML spec |
| drift | detected with `--refresh` | every plan reads the database |
| apply | resources in parallel, chained by hand | one transaction |
| scope | anything with a provider, databases and beyond | Postgres roles and privileges |
| secrets | encrypted in stack config | environment variables |

Either tool works, but only one of them should manage the roles on a given server. Pulumi fits when
database access is one part of a larger infrastructure program. pgsesame fits when the database is
the whole story and you want the plan to be SQL you can read.

::: {.chapter-notebook}
In the lab, `just sesame plan pg18` and `just sesame apply pg18` run pgsesame, and `pulumi/` holds
the Pulumi stack.
:::
